title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and m(q) output-tree parameters, and an initial state q₀ with m(q₀)=0. For each state q and input symbol σ of arity k there is at most one rule q(σ(x₁,…,x_k),y₁,…,y_m)→r. The finite right-hand side follows the grammar r ::= y_j | δ(r₁,…,r_l) | q′(x_i,r₁,…,r_{m(q′)}), with δ an output symbol of arity l and 1≤i≤k. Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input σ(t₁,…,t_k), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call q′ on the indicated child t_i with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
answer_criterion: Give an algorithm that halts with the correct equivalence answer for every pair in the stated model, or prove this decision problem undecidable. No complexity bound is requested. Decidability for restricted output growth, non-nested calls, parameter-free states or monadic input and output is insufficient. A solution for total transducers alone requires an additional reduction to cover the partial-function target as stated.
context:
A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by b(y,y) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. A decision procedure could supply finite invariants, an effective normal form or a computable completeness bound for testing; the card does not prescribe which route must work.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. It gives a powerful precedent for an invariant-based approach, but the model in that theorem is a particular tree-to-string formalism, not the unrestricted parameterized tree-to-tree model here.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

Recent progress continues on other exact properties. Gallot and Maneth’s June 2025 paper decides shape preservation for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers. Gallot, Lhote and Nguyên’s January 2026 revision decides polynomial size-to-height growth and computes its degree. These are meaningful structural classifications, but recognizing output shape or growth does not compare arbitrary output labels and positions across two transformations.

Dartois, Nguyên and Peyrat’s May 2026 paper characterizes a class of functions of linear size-to-height increase using tree-to-tree Hennie machines and a typed lambda calculus. Its equivalence proof concerns the expressive power of two models. It is not an algorithm for deciding whether two arbitrary macro tree transducers produce identical outputs. Keeping these senses of equivalence separate prevents a misleading reading of the recent abstract.

A resolution would locate an important boundary of automatic program comparison. These programs already terminate and have a disciplined recursive structure, but still support nested parameter passing and copying. Decidability would provide a foundation for validating transformations and optimizations in that model; undecidability would demonstrate that structural recursion alone does not make full semantic equality effectively recognizable.
why: Locate the decidability boundary for equivalence of terminating recursive tree programs with copying and nested output parameters.

importance.reason: A central longstanding transducer-equivalence problem, connecting functional program verification with finite-state methods, algebraic invariants and structural recursion.

progress.text: Maneth surveys decidable subclasses and identifies equivalence of unrestricted deterministic macro tree transducers as open.
Seidl–Maneth–Kemper prove deterministic top-down tree-to-string equivalence decidable through polynomial-ideal invariants.
Maneth–Seidl decide origin equivalence for weakly self-nesting macro tree transducers; ordinary unrestricted equivalence remains a distinct target.
Gallot–Maneth decide shape preservation for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers.
Gallot–Lhote–Nguyên’s revised polynomial-growth paper includes decidability and degree computation for polynomial size-to-height increase.
Dartois–Nguyên–Peyrat characterize a class of linear size-to-height functions through several models, without settling pairwise general macro-transducer equivalence.

status_note: No decision procedure or undecidability proof for the stated unrestricted deterministic macro tree-transducer equivalence problem was found through 11 September 2026. The inspected 2025–2026 results concern restricted growth, shape preservation or equivalent expressive power of models. This card specifies partial functions, inside-out semantics, ordered ranked trees and ordinary output equality.
